subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to the nebular hypothesis, the Solar System formed from which of the following?
options: A rotating cloud of gas and dust
A ring of ice ejected by the Sun
questions.explain: The nebular hypothesis states the Solar System condensed from a large rotating cloud (nebula) of gas and dust.

questions.q: Approximately how long ago did the Solar System form?
questions.explain: Evidence such as radiometric dating of meteorites gives the Solar System an age of about 4.6 billion years.

questions.q: As the nebula collapsed under gravity, it began to spin faster. This is explained by the conservation of which quantity?
questions.explain: As the cloud contracted its radius decreased, so it spun faster to conserve angular momentum.

questions.q: Why did the collapsing, spinning nebula flatten into a disc shape?
options: Because sunlight pushed the edges inward
Because of the Sun's magnetic poles
questions.explain: Rotation caused material to spread out into a flattened, spinning disc around the forming central star.

questions.q: Where did most of the mass of the collapsing nebula end up, and what did it become?
options: At the centre, forming the Sun
In the outer edge, forming comets
Spread evenly, forming the asteroid belt
In the disc, forming the gas giants
questions.explain: Most of the material concentrated at the dense, hot centre, which became the protostar and eventually the Sun.

questions.q: What event marked the point at which the central protostar became a true star (the Sun)?
options: Nuclear fusion began in its core
questions.explain: When the core became hot and dense enough, hydrogen nuclear fusion began, making it a star.

questions.q: What name is given to the disc of leftover gas and dust that surrounded the young Sun and from which the planets formed?
questions.explain: The rotating disc of leftover material around the young Sun is called the protoplanetary disc.

questions.q: What is the term for the small bodies that grew as dust grains collided and stuck together in the protoplanetary disc?
questions.explain: Grains accreted into progressively larger bodies called planetesimals, which then merged into protoplanets.

questions.q: What is the name of the process by which dust and rock grains collide and stick together to build larger bodies?
questions.explain: Accretion is the sticking together and gradual build-up of material into larger bodies.

questions.q: Why did rocky (terrestrial) planets form in the inner region of the disc, close to the Sun?
options: Only rock and metal could condense at the high temperatures there
The Sun's gravity was weaker there
Gases were attracted to the hot centre
There was more ice near the Sun
questions.explain: Near the Sun it was too hot for ices and gases to condense, so only rock and metal remained to form small dense planets.

questions.q: Beyond the 'frost line' (or snow line), volatile substances such as water could freeze into ice. How did this affect the planets that formed there?
options: It allowed large cores to grow and capture gas, forming gas giants
It stopped any planets from forming
It made the planets purely metallic
It caused those planets to spiral into the Sun
questions.explain: Beyond the frost line, abundant ices let large cores build up quickly and gather gas, producing the gas giants.

questions.q: A newly formed star blows a strong stream of particles outward, clearing much of the remaining light gas from the inner disc. What is this stream called?
questions.explain: The young Sun's solar wind swept lighter gases out of the inner Solar System, leaving rocky material behind.

questions.q: An astronomer observes a distant young star surrounded by a flattened, dusty disc with small clumps forming within it. Which stage of planet formation is this most likely showing?
options: A protoplanetary disc with planetesimals forming
A red giant shedding its outer layers
questions.explain: A dusty disc with clumps around a young star represents planetesimals accreting within a protoplanetary disc.

questions.q: What is an exoplanet?
options: A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun
A moon of a gas giant
A star that has run out of fuel
A large asteroid in the Solar System
questions.explain: An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our own Sun.

questions.q: In the transit method of detecting exoplanets, what is observed?
options: A small dip in the brightness of the star
A change in the star's colour to green
A radio signal from the planet
questions.explain: When a planet passes in front of its star, it blocks a little light, causing a small periodic dip in brightness.

questions.q: In the radial velocity (Doppler 'wobble') method, why does the star appear to wobble?
options: The gravity of the orbiting planet tugs the star back and forth
The star is physically spinning very fast
The planet emits light that pushes the star
The star is passing through a dust cloud
questions.explain: The planet and star orbit a common centre of mass, so the planet's gravity makes the star move slightly, shifting its spectral lines.

questions.q: In the radial velocity method, what happens to the star's spectral lines as it moves slightly towards and away from Earth?
options: They shift towards blue when approaching and red when receding
They only shift towards red at all times
They change from lines into a continuous rainbow
questions.explain: The Doppler effect blueshifts the light as the star approaches and redshifts it as the star recedes.

questions.q: Which was the first exoplanet discovered orbiting a Sun-like (main-sequence) star, and in which year?
questions.explain: 51 Pegasi b, found by Mayor and Queloz in 1995, was the first exoplanet detected around a Sun-like star.

questions.q: A star's brightness dips by the same small amount every 4 days with a regular, repeating pattern. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: A planet transiting the star with an orbital period of about 4 days
The star is about to become a supernova
The star is moving away from Earth
questions.explain: Regular, repeating dips in brightness indicate a transiting planet, and the interval between dips gives its orbital period.

questions.q: An astronomer wants to estimate the size (radius) of an exoplanet relative to its star. Which detection method is most directly suited to this?
options: The transit method, from the depth of the brightness dip
The radial velocity method, from the wobble speed
Listening for radio emissions from the planet
questions.explain: The fraction of light blocked during a transit depends on the planet's size, so the depth of the dip indicates its radius.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Astronomy (1AS0) specification; Formation of Planetary Systems
